title: The first sermon
hook: the middle way, the four truths, the eightfold path, at Isipatana (SN 56.11)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isipatana, the Deer Park: five doubters planned to stay seated, and then they stood up.

First speeches often vanish. The opening lecture of a new science, the first talk of a movement: nobody wrote it down, nobody knew it would matter. Buddhist tradition says it kept this one. Five men in a grove near Benares, and a man they once thought had given up is about to speak. They've agreed to listen. What he says is short, and monks still chant it. It sets out a whole path in a few plain lists.
screen: `THE FIRST THING HE SAID.` → `FIVE MEN LISTENING.` → `SHORT, AND STILL CHANTED.`

segments.voice: Dhammacakka. Dhamma is the teaching, the way things are. Cakka is a wheel. The first sermon is the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta: the teaching that set the wheel of the dhamma turning. Some readers hear in it the old Indian picture of a wheel-turning king, whose rule rolls out across the land. Here the wheel isn't an army. It's an idea set in motion. He starts, of all places, with what to avoid. Two extremes, he tells the five. One is chasing pleasure, living for the senses. The other is punishing yourself, starving, torturing the body. These five know that second road well; they walked it with him. Neither works, he says. There is a middle way. Then come the four noble truths. First: there is dukkha, the unsatisfactoriness in life: birth, aging, sickness, losing what you love, getting what you don't want. Second: it has a cause, craving, the thirst that keeps reaching. Third: it can end. When the thirst is let go, the suffering it feeds goes too. Fourth: there's a path to that end, in eight parts: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This isn't a creed about gods or a story about how the world began. Some readers hear it as a doctor's visit: the illness, the cause, the good news that it can heal, the treatment. And the wheel turns up in surprising places. There's one in the middle of India's flag. It comes from the time of Ashoka, an Indian emperor who supported the Buddhist community, and whose stone pillar stood at the Deer Park itself.
screen: `DHAMMA, THE TEACHING. CAKKA, A WHEEL.` · `TWO EXTREMES, ONE MIDDLE WAY.` · `FOUR TRUTHS, LIKE A DOCTOR'S VISIT.` · `EIGHT PARTS TO THE PATH.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL TURNS.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing that's bothering you this week, and walk it quietly through the four truths in your own words. There's this ache; it comes from wanting something to be different; it could loosen; and here's one small step toward that. No need to fix anything, just see if the shape fits.
Dhammacakka. The wheel of the dhamma: the teaching set in motion at the Deer Park, with the middle way, four truths and an eightfold path.
Your line: the wheel turns. Five men in a grove heard it first. Sixty-two days in.

howItsDone: Monks and laypeople in Theravada communities chant the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, especially on Asalha Puja, the full-moon day that remembers the first sermon, and the dharma wheel appears on temples, flags and books.

chat.says: What did the Buddha actually say in his very first talk?
options: Skip both extremes for a middle way, and four truths: suffering, cause, end, path.
Give up the world completely and starve the body until peace comes.
Life is only suffering with no way out, so expect nothing.
chat.meaning: He named two extremes to avoid, a middle way, and four noble truths: dukkha, its cause in craving, its ending, and the eightfold path.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'Think about' and drops the uncited 'two thousand years', 'ten minutes' and 'evening'; cut 'for years', 'twenty-four spokes', 'people have said for centuries' and the superlative in howItsDone. The wheel-king and doctor readings are now attributed to 'some readers'. Removed the 'Here's the practice:' opener.
The sermon is paraphrased, not quoted (Rhys Davids 1881 translated it as 'The Foundation of the Kingdom of Righteousness'; wording not quoted because not verified here).
The doctor/diagnosis analogy is described as something 'people have said for centuries'; the medical framing appears in later commentarial literature and modern scholarship. Confirm phrasing.
The Ashoka Chakra on India's flag has 24 spokes; the Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka's pillar is India's national emblem. Confirm 'set up a pillar at the Deer Park itself'.
Asalha Puja given as the festival of the first sermon in Theravada communities.
